title: Getting Others Comfortable With Disagreement
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The article addresses team members who avoid disagreement because they experience it as a personal clash rather than a clash of ideas. That avoidance keeps them out of debate and limits what they contribute. The author says leaders must help them reframe disagreement, starting with the point that decision quality falls when not all arguments are explored. A key technique is to ask them to treat disagreement as a chance to learn other perspectives and to articulate others' views, even arguing the case as an advocate would. Progress shows when they begin inviting disagreement to hear fresh ideas. The piece closes with the claim that teams get wiser when ideas clash, and that building that appreciation is a leader's job.
points: People who dread disagreement usually read it as a verdict on themselves, so the leader's task is to separate people from ideas.
Linking disagreement to decision quality gives reluctant colleagues a reason to value it.
Having reluctant colleagues state, or even advocate, others' views is a practical way to build comfort with disagreement.
A sign of progress is when these team members start inviting disagreement to hear new ideas.
quotes: When disagreed with, they feel attacked or denigrated and feel a need to defend themselves. Disagreement, in their minds, represents a clash between people, not ideas.

Working with a colleague who finds disagreement threatening begins with helping them understand the power of different points of view. Recognizing that decision quality goes down when not all of the ideas and arguments are explored gives them a better appreciation for why disagreement is so essential.

Those who find disagreement unsavory typically believe it is a struggle between right and wrong, or good and bad. They personalize attacks on ideas, believing differences in opinion impugn the advocate. Giving them an alternate frame helps them to see disagreement differently.

Asking these colleagues to see disagreement as a learning opportunity where they can experience other perspectives and viewpoints is critical. Request that they give up their strong allegiance to any particular idea and to enter the discussion with curiosity to learn how others see the issue.

Suddenly, they begin to see disagreement as less about them and more about ideas and content. Leaders know they have made progress when these team members begin to invite disagreement, hoping to hear fresh ideas about an issue.

Showing them the power of disagreement to improve the thinking of the entire team and asking each and every team member to engage fully when they disagree are table stakes for making quality decisions. We become wiser together when our ideas clash. Getting everyone to appreciate that is what good leaders do.
